docs.title: Automated Harvesting of Leafy Green Vegetables
docs.text:
Design and development of a row-based automated harvesting system for hydroponically grown leafy vegetables in indoor vertical farms.

Your browser does not support HTML5 video.

Produced by: Clement Joshua Dev, Saiful Imran and Ong Qi Zhi Ignatius

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text:
This project investigates the design and development of an automated harvesting system for leafy green vegetables cultivated in hydroponic trays.

The proposed system combines mechanical leaf support, opposing cup-shaped grippers, a cutting mechanism, and coordinated row-based harvesting to reduce manual intervention during harvesting.

docs.title: Project Objectives
docs.text:
1. Develop an automated harvesting mechanism for leafy green vegetables.

  2. Minimise mechanical damage during crop handling and separation.

  3. Enable simultaneous row-based harvesting using coordinated mechanical actuation.

  4. Evaluate design feasibility through prototyping and functional testing.

docs.title: 8.1 Appendix A: Jet Calculations for Four Pressure Washers
docs.text:
The relations presented in Section 3.7.2 were applied to each pressure washer using its maximum rated pressure and flow rate. The calculations assume that the entire flow is directed through a single nozzle, with negligible losses.

The equivalent stress was calculated by distributing the jet impact force over the cross-sectional area of a 10 mm diameter lettuce stem (78.5 mm²), following the impact model adopted by the IS-404 Team (2026).

The reference design stress is 0.30 MPa, based on a failure stress of 0.20 MPa and a safety factor of 1.5.

docs.title: 2.1 Systematic Ideation
docs.text:
The design process began with a brainstorming exercise conducted using Miro, an online collaborative whiteboard. The team identified challenges associated with harvesting leafy green vegetables and proposed a range of unconventional solutions using virtual sticky notes. These ideas were deliberately exaggerated or impractical to encourage creative thinking without being constrained by technical feasibility during the initial ideation stage.

Fig. 2.1. Miro Board Ideation

From the identified harvesting challenges, five promising yet unconventional ideas were shortlisted for further development. Each idea was paired with a specific harvesting problem and arranged according to its degree of unconventionality.

The shortlisted ideas underwent an iterative refinement process involving five approaches: pivoting the original concept, reducing its complexity, incorporating existing technologies, improving ease of adoption by farms, and simplifying operation. Through this process, the initial ideas were progressively transformed into more practical mechanical solutions.

For example, the proposed use of water pistols to separate lettuce stems evolved into fixed waterjet nozzles, while an oversized fork intended to scoop entire lettuce heads was refined into smaller tines capable of sliding beneath the leaves to support the crop. Similarly, the idea of using an animal to reach elevated growing racks contributed to the development of a conveyor-based approach for positioning cultivation trays.

Fig. 2.2. Iterative refinement of unconventional ideas

These refined ideas formed the basis for subsequent concept generation, with several features incorporated into the proposed harvesting mechanisms.

docs.title: 2.2 Morphological Analysis
docs.text:
Following the initial ideation exercise, a morphological chart was developed to systematically explore alternative harvesting mechanisms. The overall harvesting operation was decomposed into five sub-functions:

  1. Presenting the crop to the machine,
  2. Locating individual rows,
  3. Separating the crop from the growing tray,
  4. Lifting the harvested crop, and
  5. Releasing it from the mechanism.

For each sub-function, the team brainstormed and sketched multiple potential solutions. These included mechanisms adapted from existing technologies as well as original concepts developed during the ideation process.

Fig. 2.3. Morphological Chart

By combining different solutions across the sub-functions, four distinct harvesting concepts were developed:

  1. Concept A — Fork-Lift Harvester: Uses mechanical tines to support and lift lettuce heads along a cultivation row.

  2. Concept B — Robotic Pick-and-Place: Employs a robotic manipulator and end-effector to handle individual crops.

  3. Concept C — Continuous Clamp Belt: Uses opposing moving belts to grip and transport harvested crops.

  4. Concept D — Waterjet and Vacuum Entry: Combines waterjet cutting with vacuum-assisted crop handling.

Fig. 2.4. Four harvesting concepts generated from the morphological chart

These concepts were subsequently evaluated to identify the most suitable approach for further development.

docs.title: 2.3 Concept Evaluation and Selection
docs.text:
Following the morphological analysis, four harvesting concepts were evaluated using a weighted decision matrix to identify the most suitable design for further development. Each concept was assessed against six criteria: crop damage, throughput, cost and part count, reliability and control simplicity, hygiene, and compatibility with standard cultivation trays.

Greater weight was assigned to crop damage (25%), throughput (20%), and cost (20%), reflecting the importance of maintaining crop quality while achieving efficient and economically viable harvesting operations. The remaining criteria comprised reliability and control simplicity (15%), hygiene (10%), and tray compatibility (10%).

Each concept was rated on a scale of 1 to 5, with the individual scores multiplied by their respective criterion weights to obtain an overall weighted score.

The fork-lift harvester (Concept A) achieved the highest weighted score of 4.10 out of 5, followed by the continuous clamp belt (Concept C) at 3.25, robotic pick-and-place system (Concept B) at 2.90, and waterjet gantry (Concept D) at 2.80.

Fig. 2.5. (a) Concept evaluation criteria and weightings, (b) Weighted scores of the four harvesting concepts.

Concept A was selected as the preferred design due to its ability to support and harvest an entire row of leafy vegetables simultaneously without directly gripping the leaves. Its relatively simple mechanical arrangement also offered potential advantages in throughput, control complexity, and minimising crop damage.

The selected concept subsequently served as the foundation for further design refinement and integration with complementary harvesting mechanisms.

docs.title: 2.4 Final Concept Development
docs.text:
Although Concept A achieved the highest overall evaluation score, certain features from the other concepts were identified as beneficial for further development. In particular, the waterjet cutting mechanism from Concept D was incorporated into the selected fork-lift harvester to form a hybrid design.

The hybrid concept retains the fork-lifting mechanism to support the leafy vegetables from below, while incorporating fixed waterjet nozzles to separate the stems. Unlike Concept D, which proposed a moving waterjet gantry, the hybrid design eliminates the need for an additional gantry axis by positioning the cutting nozzles at fixed locations.

During subsequent design refinement, opposing cup-shaped grippers were introduced beneath the fork structure to provide additional stabilisation around the base of each vegetable. The cups are designed to approach the plant from opposite sides, providing a larger contact area while avoiding direct compression of the leaves.

To accommodate simultaneous row-based harvesting, the cup-shaped grippers are intended to operate through a shared actuation mechanism. This allows multiple gripping units to be synchronised using a common drive system, reducing the need for individual actuators.

The resulting design combines fork-based leaf support, cup-shaped crop stabilisation, and waterjet cutting within a coordinated harvesting system. The detailed design of these mechanisms is presented in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 2.5 Summary of Final Design
docs.text:
The refined harvesting system integrates a fork-lifting mechanism, opposing cup-shaped grippers, a waterjet cutting system, conveyor belt, comb strips, and gravity chute to facilitate simultaneous harvesting of leafy green vegetables along a cultivation row.

The proposed harvesting sequence begins with the conveyor belt positioning the cultivation tray relative to the harvesting mechanism. The fork tines are then positioned beneath the lettuce leaves to provide support, while the opposing cup-shaped grippers approach the base of each plant to stabilise the crop during harvesting.

Once the vegetables are secured, the fixed waterjet nozzles cut the stems to separate them from their growing trays. Following separation, the harvested vegetables are transferred from the supporting structure using comb strips and directed towards the collection area through a gravity chute. The sequence is repeated as subsequent rows are positioned for harvesting.

The cup-shaped grippers are designed to operate through a shared actuation mechanism, enabling multiple harvesting units to grip their respective crops simultaneously. This arrangement aims to reduce the number of independently controlled actuators while maintaining coordinated handling across a cultivation row.

By combining row-based leaf support, controlled crop stabilisation, and fixed waterjet cutting, the proposed system aims to improve harvesting efficiency while minimising mechanical damage to the vegetables. The detailed mechanical design, component specifications, and integration of these mechanisms are discussed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: conclusion
docs.text: Harvesting remains the manual stage at ArianeTech and across Singapore’s vertical farms, and gripping the leaves is the main source of crop damage. Through systematic ideation, a morphological chart and weighted scoring, the team selected a fork-lift harvester with a fixed waterjet, then refined it through four virtual iterations. Each iteration removed a weakness of the last: the flip and comb, the loose heads, and finally the drop into a chute. The final design, Harvester_v2, holds each head by the base of its stem in a split cup, gathers the leaves with S-curved tines, cuts a whole row with one jet and sets the heads down on the tray. Its simulated rate of about 1,350 heads per hour is 13–18 times the observed manual rate. The critical unknown is whether an affordable pump can cut the stems; Semester 2 will answer it by test, alongside safe cup force and an integrated trial with ArianeTech lettuce.

docs.title: 3.1 Ideation
docs.text:
Using a Miro board, we brainstormed ideas and solutions on virtual sticky notes. From the "difficult" board, we picked our five most useful "lousy" ideas. Each one pairs a silly solution with a problem, and we sorted them by how unusual they are (Figure 2). We then pushed each idea through an iteration process: pivot it, reduce its ambition, build it from things that already exist, make it easier for a farm to adopt, and make it easier to use (Figure 3). The two best ideas were then chosen and pitched (Figure 4).

Figure 2: Miro board: why lettuce picking is difficult (yellow) and deliberately "lousy" solutions (green).

Figure 3: Iterating the lousy ideas: pivot, reduce the ambition, build from what exists, ease adoption and use.

Figure 4: Choosing the two best ideas and pitching them.

Every main part of our CAD and designs can be traced back to an idea on this board (Figure 5):

  • The conveyor belt indexes a tray forward until a photo eye detects the edge of the tray.
  • The water pistols became off-the-shelf water nozzles that cut the stem cleanly.
  • The giant forks became small tines that slide in between the stems and underneath the lettuce heads.

Figure 5: From lousy idea to final part: each main component traces back to the ideation board.

docs.title: 3.2 Functional Decomposition and Concept Selection
docs.text:
We then moved on to the morphological chart, where the team broke the harvesting task down into sub-functions: presenting the crop to the machine, locating each row, freeing the head from the tray, raising it clear, releasing it from the end effector, moving it to collection, and storing it (Figure 6). For each sub-function, we brainstormed and sketched as many ways of doing it as we could. Some came from existing solutions and others were our own ideas.

Figure 6: Morphological chart: options for each of the seven sub-functions, with the chosen path highlighted.

By tracing different paths through the chart, we came up with four concepts (Figure 7):

  • (A) Fork-lift harvester
  • (B) Robot pick and place
  • (C) Continuous clamp belt
  • (D) Waterjet and vacuum entry

Figure 7: Concept sheets for the leading solutions.

We scored each concept from 1 to 5 against weighted criteria: crop damage (25%), throughput (20%), cost and part count (20%), reliability and simple control (15%), hygiene (10%) and fit with standard trays (10%). Figure 8 shows the weighted totals: the fork-lift harvester scored 4.10, ahead of the clamp belt (3.25), the robot arm (2.90) and the waterjet gantry (2.80). Crop damage carries the largest weight because a damaged head is lost revenue.

The fork-lift harvester came out best because it was the only concept that clears a whole row at once without grippers. The selected design combined concept A with the waterjet cut from concept D, but dropped D's moving gantry so that the jet stays fixed.

Figure 8: Criteria weights and weighted scores out of 5 for the four concepts.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Concept
docs.text:
Design 1 combines the fork-lift harvester with the waterjet cut from the waterjet gantry concept. The fork lifts a row of lettuce from below, a fixed waterjet cuts the stems, and a comb strips the heads into a gravity chute. The moving gantry from the waterjet concept was dropped, so the jet stays in one place. The waterjet was kept because it cuts without touching the leaves, and in other harvesting methods gripping causes most of the damage [10].

Design 1 has six components: a conveyor that indexes the trays, the fork, the fixed waterjet, a lift, stripper comb strips, and a gravity chute into a collection bin (Figure 9). In one cycle the row slides onto the tines, the fork lifts it and turns 135°, and the comb strips the heads down the chute into the bin (Figure 10).

Figure 9: Design 1 in SolidWorks: conveyor, fork on the lift unit, stripper comb, discharge chute and bin.

Figure 10: One cycle of Design 1 (anatomy model, 135° turn).

docs.title: 3.3.2 Fork Specifications
docs.text:
The fork has to support each lettuce without gripping it, fit between adjacent rows and carry the full mass of the plant. Its dimensions come from the lettuce measurements in Table 1 and from simulation (Table 3).

Table 3: Fork dimensions and their basis.

Parameter Basis Value Tine gap (T) Leaf spread of about 330 mm divided by 4 ≈ 76 mm Maximum tine gap The fork must not hit lettuce in adjacent rows T < 280 mm Tine width 14.45 ÷ 2π = 14.45 ÷ 6.283 ≈ 23 mm Tine length (L) L ≥ 4D, where D = 79.5 mm from simulation ≥ 318 mm (4 × 79.5 mm)

The final design rounds the calculated values and keeps the tine length, width and gap in a ratio of 320 : 23 : 75 (Table 4).

Table 4: Final fork dimensions.

Dimension Value Tine length 320 mm Tine width 23 mm Tine gap 75 mm

docs.title: 3.3.3 CAD and Assembly
docs.text:
The fork has a steerer tube, headset cups, a crown, tines, and holes for the waterjet stream (Figure 11). The parts were modelled in SolidWorks from sketches with extrude, revolve and reference-geometry features.

Figure 11: Fork parts (left) and fork CAD (right).

The assembly was built from the bottom up, with mates only where parts move. Parts that never move, such as the rotor shaft, head tubes and forks, were placed at exact coordinates and fixed.

Lift unit. The rotor axis and the bearing axis are coincident, so the shaft is centred in its bearings and can only spin or slide along its length. The rotor's front plane is coincident with the lift unit's front plane, which stops the sliding (Figure 12). The lift unit has two positions in the simulation (Figure 13, Table 5).

Figure 12: Lift unit: rotor gearmotor, shaft, lift carriage and tines.

Figure 13: Lift unit at the harvest position (left) and the strip position (right).

Table 5: Lift-unit positions in the simulation.

1: Harvest 2: Strip Rotor height 526 mm 885 mm Fork angle Level Turned 135° During simulation Jet cuts; heads on the forks Heads slide off the comb

Frame. In the full machine the lift unit is attached to the blue frame (Figure 14). A coincident front plane stops it drifting sideways across the belt, and a coincident right plane stops it drifting along the conveyor. A distance mate sets the rotor height for each position, and a parallel mate between a rotor plane and a frame plane sets the fork angle.

Figure 14: Blue frame carrying the lift unit.

Interference detection. To find places where two parts overlap, the angle plane was turned through 360° in 15° steps, which turns the fork with it. At each step the team checked whether the fork touches the frame or the stripper combs.

docs.title: 3.3.4 Problems Found in Virtual Testing
docs.text:
The CAD review identified two concerns with the fork mechanism (Figure 15):

  1. Range of motor angle. A full 360° rotation allows continuous movement in one direction, but requires enough clearance around the shaft to prevent the tines from striking the frame or comb. The interference check therefore covered the complete rotation. Limiting movement to 135° before reversing reduces the swept space, but requires controlled endpoints and repeated direction changes.
  2. Comb sticking. The comb introduces a separate concern, as wet leaves could become trapped between its teeth and the fork during discharge.

Together, these issues prompted a closer review of how the mechanism handles each head throughout the cycle.

Figure 15: Questions raised by Design 1: the range of motor angle, and wet heads sticking between comb and fork.

The anatomy model (Figure 10) revealed three further weaknesses:

  • No restraint. The heads have no restraint as the fork lifts and rotates, leaving them vulnerable to slipping.
  • Disordered output. The heads roll down the chute and collect in a heap, adding handling before packing. Greenphyto's continued use of manual harvesting highlights the importance of orderly, pack-ready output [14].
  • Actuator count. Separate actuators increase coordination and maintenance demands.

Design 2 was developed to improve head retention, discharge control and mechanical simplicity.

docs.title: 3.4 Design 2: Two-Axis Gantry
docs.text:
Design 2 replaces the rotating fork and comb with a two-axis gantry above the conveyor's discharge end (Figure 16). The fork slides beneath the front row while a fixed waterjet cuts the stems. It then lifts the heads level and moves horizontally over the chute for release. Table 6 compares this arrangement with Design 1, building on the evaluation presented at the interim presentation.

Figure 16: One cycle of Design 2 (anatomy model, rear isometric view).

Table 6: Design 1 (one gantry axis with a flip) compared with Design 2 (two-axis gantry).

Aspect Design 1: one axis + flip Design 2: two-axis gantry Motors One lift axis plus a rotor for the flip Two gantry axes, vertical and horizontal Control 360° continuous, or 135° with stop and reversal Two axes must be coordinated; standard Cartesian motion Head orientation Tipped 135°; heads slide off under gravity Level throughout Release Comb strips the heads; wet leaves may wedge No comb; heads released over the chute Swept space Tines sweep an arc around the shaft Rectangular envelope above the conveyor Frame Compact single portal Larger portal with two rails Remaining risks Heads unrestrained during motion; drop into chute and bin Same: heads unrestrained; drop into chute and bin

Design 2 removes the rotational clearance and comb concerns, but adds a larger frame and a second coordinated axis. The heads remain loose on the tines and drop onto a chute during discharge. This shifted the focus towards supporting each head securely through cutting, transfer and release.

docs.title: 3.5.1 Single Cup
docs.text:
Design 3 replaces the open tines with a split, funnel-shaped cup beneath the lettuce head, flanked by two S-curved guide rails (Figure 17). As the plant advances, the rails guide the outer leaves upward and inward to ease entry into the cup (Figure 18). A rack-and-pinion mechanism closes the cup halves around the stem before the waterjet cuts below, leaving the lower stem and roots on the conveyor while supporting the head upright.

This arrangement shifts support from the leaves to the base, responding to the gripping injuries reported by Ma et al. [10]. Retaining the head after cutting also addresses the toppling problem described by a tray-harvester manufacturer [15], providing a basis for controlled transfer.

Figure 17: Design 3 CAD: early holder with S-curved arms and rail (top left), split cup on a rack and pinion (bottom left), refined holder (right).

Figure 18: One cycle of the single-cup holder (anatomy model).

docs.title: 3.5.2 Multiple Cups
docs.text:
The multi-cup arrangement extends the single-head concept to four cups on a shared rack, each with its own pair of S-curved rails (Figure 19). One pinion closes the cups together, while a common waterjet line cuts beneath the stems. This restores row-by-row harvesting with one closing actuator while retaining individual support for each head during cutting.

Figure 19: One cycle of the multi-cup holder (anatomy model).

docs.title: 3.6 Harvester_v2: Automated Lettuce Harvester without Lift
docs.text:
The final design builds the multi-cup holder into a station over the conveyor (Figure 20). Its key parameters are listed in Table 7, and one cycle from the SolidWorks motion study is shown in Figure 21.

Figure 20: Harvester in SolidWorks: station over the conveyor (top left), half-cups between S-curved tines (top right), heads in the holders (bottom left) and cut head tipped onto the tray (bottom right).

Table 7: Key parameters of Harvester_v2 (from the CAD model).

Parameter Value Holders per row Three half-cup pairs at 300 mm pitch, matching the row pitch of the CAD tray model Drive One gearmotor pinion between two opposed racks, so both halves close symmetrically Cup Revolved funnel: about 21–26 mm inner diameter at the stem, 111–116 mm at the rim Cup travel Open 64 mm per side; entry 22 mm per side (44 mm gap); closed Leaf guide S-curved tine rail rising from 40 mm to 114 mm above the tray Cut One waterjet sweeping 22 mm upward through the stem zone below the cups Release Cups open; each head tips forward about 65° onto the tray beside its stub Indexing Conveyor advances 300 mm per row Simulated cycle About 8 s per row of three

Figure 21: One cycle of Harvester_v2 from the SolidWorks motion study.

In each cycle:

  1. The tray indexes the next row in while the cups are half-closed.
  2. The S-rails lift the leaves, and the stems slide into the 44 mm entry gap.
  3. The racks close the cups.
  4. The jet cuts the stems.
  5. The cups open, and each head tips forward onto the tray with its roots exposed.
  6. The row moves on.

The motion study was checked frame by frame so that no part passes through another, and the tipped head comes to rest about 0.5 mm above the tray. The head never leaves the tray's support, so there is no drop into a chute.

Throughput

At about 8 s per row of three, the simulated rate is 3 × 3,600 ÷ 8 ≈ 1,350 heads per hour. That is about 13–18 times the observed manual rate of 75–100 heads per hour, within the 10–40× target set in Section 2.3. The cycle time is a motion-study assumption that must be confirmed on hardware.

Closing force

Because one pinion drives both racks, the closing force is set by motor torque: F = T / r. With a pitch radius of 10 mm and three cups per rack, limiting each cup to a force Fc requires T = 3 Fc r. For an illustrative Fc of 2 N this is only 0.06 N·m. Crop safety therefore depends on limiting motor current, not on motor size. The safe value of Fc is unknown and is the target of test T2 (Section 5).

Table 8: How each design answered the weakness of the one before.

Design What it fixed What it left open 1: Fork lift + flip Clears a whole row at once without grippers Lift actuator; loose heads; comb sticking; drop into chute and bin 2: Two-axis gantry No flip, no comb; heads stay level Two coordinated motors; heads still loose; still a drop 3: Single cup Head gathered and held gently through the cut One head per cycle 3: Multi-cup A row per cycle with one drive and one jet Release path; even closing; jet sizing Final: Harvester_v2 Opposed racks on one pinion; heads stay on the tray, no drop Jet pressure, cup force and release still to be tested

docs.title: 3.7.2 Jet Calculations
docs.text:
In 2013, UC Davis and Fresh Express ran two trials comparing knife cutting with waterjet cutting of salad-cut romaine [20]. Lettuce was cut into 2-inch pieces, bagged in air and stored at 2.5 °C for up to 20 days, then scored for visual quality, discoloration and whitening of the cut edges. Waterjet-cut romaine kept better cut-surface quality than blade-cut romaine (Figure 22) [21]. The trials used an industrial waterjet pump at 35,000–55,000 psi (about 2,400–3,800 bar), far above the 100–145 bar of the washers in Table 9, so the jet for this design has to be sized separately.

Figure 22: Blade-cut and waterjet-cut romaine after 8 and 18 days of storage (UC Davis and Fresh Express trials; KMT Waterjet, 2013 [20]).

These figures assume each washer runs at its maximum pressure and maximum flow at the same time, with no losses in the hose or nozzle and one nozzle taking the whole flow. Pressure P is in pascals (1 bar = 100,000 Pa), flow Q is in m³/s (1 L/min = 1/60,000 m³/s) and water density ρ is 1000 kg/m³.

  • Jet velocity: v = √(2P / ρ)
  • Hydraulic power: P × Q
  • Equivalent nozzle diameter: d = √(4Q / (π × v))
  • Jet force on the target: F = ρ × Q × v

Worked example, Makita HW102 (100 bar, 6 L/min):

  • v = √(2 × 10,000,000 ÷ 1000) ≈ 141 m/s
  • Hydraulic power = 10,000,000 Pa × 0.0001 m³/s = 1,000 W
  • Nozzle diameter = √(4 × 0.0001 ÷ (π × 141)) ≈ 0.95 mm
  • Jet force = 1000 × 0.0001 × 141 ≈ 14 N

Applying the same relations to all four washers gives jet forces of 14–24 N when one nozzle takes the full flow (Appendix A, Table 13).

The previous cohort estimated, with an impact-stress model, that a 0.5 mm nozzle needs about 74 MPa to sever a 10 mm stem, assuming a tissue failure stress of 0.20 MPa and a safety factor of 1.5 [22]. That is 7.4 times the HW102's 10 MPa. On the same model, the HW102's full 14 N spread over a 10 mm stem gives 0.18 MPa, below the 0.30 MPa design stress, and sharing the flow among three stems lowers it further.

Commercial waterjet harvesters do cut whole romaine in the field [23], so the model is probably conservative: a jet cuts by eroding a narrow kerf rather than loading the whole cross-section. Pressure, nozzle size and stand-off must therefore be found by test (T1) before a pump is chosen.

docs.title: 1.1 Singapore's Food Security
docs.text:
Singapore relies heavily on imported food to meet domestic consumption needs, with over 90% of its food supply sourced internationally [1]. This dependence exposes the country to external supply disruptions arising from climate change, geopolitical developments, and interruptions to international supply chains.

To strengthen national food resilience, Singapore has adopted a multi-pronged strategy encompassing import diversification, global partnerships, stockpiling, and local food production [1].

However, expanding domestic agricultural production presents significant challenges due to Singapore's limited land availability. Historical estimates indicate that agricultural land declined from approximately 15,000 hectares in the 1960s to around 600 hectares by 2019 [2].

Consequently, space-efficient agricultural technologies, such as indoor vertical farming, offer a potential means of increasing local food production without requiring a proportional increase in land use.

docs.title: 1.2 Indoor Vertical Farming in Singapore
docs.text:
Vertical Farming offers an alternative to converntional land-based agriculture by cultivating crops in vertically stacked layers. In 2011, Singapore's Sky Greens developed the "A-Go-Gro" - a rotating vertical A-frame structure supporting tiers of vegetable trays. The system reported to achieve yields of up to ten times those of conventional farmland per unit area [3].

Fig. 1. Sky Greens A-Go-Gro vertical farming system. Image source: [4].

Modern Vertical Farms use controlled-environment technologies like artificial lighting, climate control and recirculating hydroponic systems to regulate growing conditions [5]. These technologies enable consistent, year-round cultivation by reducing dependence on external environmental conditions.

Indoor vertical farming can improve water-use efficiency. Hydroponic systems reduce water losses through drip irrigation and recirculating nutrients solutions, with reported water savigns reaching up to 95% compared with traditional cultivation under controlled conditions [6].

Fig. 2. Recirculating Hydroponics System. Image source: [7].

Leafy green vegetables, such as lettuce and bok choy, are particularly relevant to indoor vertical farming due to their relatively short cultivation cycles and suitablilty for hydroponic growing systems [8]

docs.title: 1.3 Automation in Indoor Farming
docs.text:
Automation can improve operational efficiency of indoor vertical farms by reducing manual intervention in repetitive processes.

ArianeTech, our industry partner for this project, is a Singapore-based agricultural technology solutions provider specialising in indoor vertical farming systems. The company offers integrates solutions incorporating automted cultivation systems and equipment like smart environmental control systems [9].

For the cultivation of leafy green vegetables, a typical production workflow can be simplified into four main stages: seeding, transplantion, cultivation, and harvesting. ArianeTech offers solutions that automate the first four stages, while harvesting remains the focus for automation development.

Fig. 3. Illustration of automated technologies used in seeding, transplanting and contolled-environment cultivation in indoor vertical farming.

As the capacity for cultivation increases, the reliance on manual harvesting may constrain production throughput and increase labour requirements. Developing an automated harvesting system presents an opportunity to improve the scalability and operational efficiency of indoor vertical farming.

docs.title: 1.4 Challenges of Manual Harvesting
docs.text:
Harvesting leafy green vegetables is not straightforward delicate physical structure and variations in plant geometry. Ma et al. investigated flexible finger gripping of hydroponic lettuce and reported injured leaf areas ranging from 120.3 mm² to 275.5 mm² across different gripping configurations [10]. This demonstrates the importance of controlling contact forces and gripping positions to minimise crop damage.

Manual harvesting also presents challenges in terms of labour productivity and scalability. Ohayama er al, evaluated an artifically illuminated lettuce production facility and reported labout productivy ranging from 1.5 to 6.0 kg per person-hour, with harvesting identified as the most time-consuming production operation [11]. Furthermore, Agrilyst's 2017 industrry survey found that labour accounted for 56% of operation expenses among surveyed indoor vertical farms [12].

As production capacity increases, dependence on manual harvesting may constrain throughput and increase labour requirements. These findings highlight the potential value of developing automated harvesting systems that minimise crop damage while enabling scalability.

docs.title: 1.5 Problem Statement
docs.text:
Despite advancements in the automation of indoor vertical farming, harvesting remains a labour-intensive operation within the production workflow considered in this project. As cultivation capacity increases, reliance on manual harvesting may limit production throughput, creating a bottleneck in an otherwise automated production process.

Therefore, there is a need to develop an automated harvesting system capable of handling leafy green vegetables of different geometries and qualities, efficiently and consistently, with minimal crop damage. The proposed system should also accommodate simultaneous harvesting along cultivation rows to support scalability in indoor vertical farming operations.

docs.title: 1.6.1 Project Objectives
docs.text:
The primary objective of this project is to design and develop an automated harvesting system for leafy green vegetables cultivated in hydroponic trays within indoor vertical farms.

The specific objectives are to:

  1. Develop an automated harvesting mechanism capable of separating and collecting mature leafy green vegetables from their growing trays.

  2. Minimise mechanical damage to crops through suitable handling, supporting, and cutting mechanisms that accommodate variations in plant geometry.

  3. Enable simultaneous row-based harvesting through a mechanically synchronised system to improve harvesting efficiency and scalability.

  4. Evaluate the feasibility of the proposed design through mechanical analysis, prototyping, and functional testing.

docs.title: 1.6.2 Project Scope
docs.text:
This project focuses on the mechanical design and development of an automated harvesting system for leafy green vegetables grown in hydroponic trays. The proposed system encompasses three primary operations: supporting and handling mature crops, separating the vegetables from their stems or root systems, and transferring the harvested produce for further processing.

The design emphasises simultaneous harvesting along a cultivation row rather than individual crop harvesting. Particular consideration is given to minimising crop damage, simplifying mechanical actuation, and ensuring compatibility with the existing cultivation arrangement.

The project includes concept generation and evaluation, detailed mechanical design, prototype fabrication, and functional testing to assess the feasibility of the proposed harvesting system. The development of a fully integrated, commercial-scale harvesting system is beyond the scope of this project.

docs.title: 2.1 Objective
docs.text:
The objective is to design and evaluate a harvesting module that separates whole lettuce heads from their roots at the end of ArianeTech's existing tray conveyor, faster than manual harvesting and without gripping the leaves. In Semester 1 the team:

  1. analysed the manual workflow and located the bottleneck,
  2. generated and selected concepts systematically, and
  3. developed the selected concept through four design iterations, checked in CAD, anatomy animations and SolidWorks motion studies.

Semester 2 will build and test physical prototypes.

docs.title: 2.2 System Context and Project Scope
docs.text:
The module sits between the cultivation racks and packing. Its input is a tray of mature lettuce arriving on a conveyor; its output is a row of cut heads ready to be collected, with the root stubs left in the tray.

  • In scope: presenting each row, holding the heads, cutting the stems and releasing the heads.
  • Out of scope: retrieving trays from the racks, packing and tray washing.

Two interface rules come from the partner: the module must accept the farm's trays without modification, and unintended crop damage must be kept to a minimum [22].

docs.title: 2.3 Design Estimates
docs.text:
The harvesting mechanism must accommodate differences in lettuce size and weight while supporting the leaves gently during collection. Published measurements of hydroponic lettuce provided the initial design values, alongside observations made during the ArianeTech industry visit. These findings guided the working clearance, carrying capacity and contact arrangement summarised in Table 1.

Table 1: Physical attributes of hydroponic lettuce and the design conclusions drawn from them.

Attribute Research-supported value Design conclusion Plant height Height ranged from 161–212 mm, with a mean of 185.8 mm [13, Table 1]. Provide adjustable height and sufficient clearance for the tallest plants in the intended crop. Leaf droop Observed during the ArianeTech industry visit. Use a narrow insertion profile to reach beneath the leaves. Determine the insertion height through measurements of ArianeTech's lettuce. Plant mass Mass ranged from 113.23–196.36 g with roots and 102.45–179.67 g after root removal [13, Table 1]. Adopt 230 g as the initial design payload and check carrying performance during lifting and transfer. Extraction force from planting board Extraction required 9.6–16.5 N, with a mean of 13.03 N [13, Sec. 3.3]. Account for extraction resistance when sizing the lifting mechanism and secure the planting board against upward movement. Leaf injury during gripping Tested flexible-finger configurations recorded forces of approximately 1.67–2.33 N per finger and mean leaf injury areas of 120.3–275.5 mm² [10, Tables 3–4]. Spread the contact load and limit squeezing of the leaves. Refine contact position and applied force through handling trials. Moisture content Average moisture content was 95.73% in leaves and 91.71% in stems [13, Table 2]. Keep the transfer from harvesting to packing short. Check slipping and sticking on the selected contact material using lettuce in its actual harvesting condition. Canopy diameter Diameter ranged from 282–378 mm, with a mean of 331.6 mm [13, Table 1]. Allow sufficient clearance around the canopy and set fork spacing according to the region supporting the plant.

docs.title: Design requirements from lettuce
docs.text:
• Load: size carrying components for a 230 g payload, above the measured maximum of 196 g, and validate this allowance on ArianeTech's crop.
  • Contact: flexible fingers applying about 2 N per finger still injured leaves [10]. Support the head without squeezing its leaves and refine contact force through testing.
  • Cut before lifting: extraction requires 9.6–16.5 N [13], substantially exceeding the head's weight. The selected sequence cuts the stem before lifting to avoid this extraction load.
  • Edges: round tine and cup edges to distribute contact loads and reduce snagging.
  • Size range: accommodate heights of 161–212 mm and canopy diameters of 282–378 mm.

These requirements guide individual handling, while throughput determines overall capacity.

docs.title: Throughput target
docs.text: The preliminary cost model targets 750–4,000 heads per hour, spanning 10 times the lower observed manual rate of 75 heads per hour to 40 times the upper rate of 100. The team will refine this target with ArianeTech.

docs.title: 2.4 Existing Solutions
docs.text:
Table 2 summarises the solutions reviewed, from laboratory grippers to commercial lines.

Table 2: Existing harvesting solutions and why none fits the problem as posed.

Solution What it does Limitation for this project Soft-finger gripper [10] Uses flexible fingers to grasp and lift hydroponic lettuce. Leaf injury occurred at approximately 2 N per finger, highlighting the need to control contact force and position. Twisted double-belt clamp [24] Clamps and conveys rows of spinach, with reported harvesting success of 94% and damage of 3%. Applies approximately 2.37 N of clamping force. Its suitability for delicate lettuce heads requires testing. FingerVision robot [25] Cuts lettuce on growing plates and transfers each head using a gripper with visual and tactile sensing. Handles one head per cycle and relies on direct gripping, requiring assessment against the project's throughput and damage targets. Hortiplan Harvest Automation [26] Lifts plants out of gutters, then cuts. Designed around gutters and would require adaptation to ArianeTech's trays. Sormac CEA harvester [27] Uses airflow to raise leaves for cutting by two circular knives, processing up to 80 gutters per hour. Designed for harvesting leaves rather than supporting and transferring intact heads. Cutting blades serve multiple plants. Ramsay Highlander [23] Uses waterjets to cut six rows of field-grown romaine in one pass. Designed for open-field harvesting and still relies on 12 workers to handle the cut heads. Hamill tray harvester [15], [28] Cuts microgreens grown in trays, with a reported cutting time of approximately three seconds per tray. Whole lettuce heads need additional support after cutting to prevent toppling. IS-404 [22] Proposes tray separation, plant clamping and waterjet root detachment in the previous cohort's design. The estimated waterjet pressure of 74 MPa and its performance on planted trays require experimental validation.

The reviewed solutions highlight the importance of gentle support and clean cutting. Gripping can injure leaves, while field applications demonstrate waterjet cutting of whole lettuce. UC Davis trials also reported better cut-surface quality in waterjet-cut romaine than in blade-cut samples [21]. These findings guide the project towards supporting each head throughout cutting without squeezing its leaves. Combining this approach with ArianeTech's existing trays forms the focus of the proposed harvesting module.

docs.title: 4. Shortcomings
docs.text:
In Semester 1, project evaluation has involved the design and development of CAD models, anatomy models, motion studies and physical prototype testing. Table 10 summarises the remaining shortcomings and the planned improvements that will guide the next stage of development.

Table 10: Shortcomings of the current design and proposed resolutions.

Shortcoming Why it matters Proposed resolution Jet pressure unproven A 10 MPa washer is 7.4× below the 74 MPa estimate Cut tests over pressure, nozzle and stand-off (T1) One jet in line with three stems The first stem may shield the others until it is severed Test sweep speed; compare one nozzle per stem Safe cup force unknown Over-closing could bruise the stem base Measure force against bruising (T2); current-limit the motor Collection after release Heads lie tipped on the tray; packing is not yet designed Define hand-off with ArianeTech; assess landing damage (T3) Tray layout The CAD tray uses rows of three at 300 mm; ArianeTech's layout must be confirmed Measure partner trays; adjust cup count and pitch Hygiene and water containment Jet spray and cut juice must not contaminate the crop Splash guard, food-grade contact parts, drainage Conveyor drive Motor type and motion when the holder engages are undecided Compare stepper and gearmotor drives during T4

The tests T1–T4 referred to above are described in the Semester 2 test plan (Section 5).

docs.title: Mechanism Design
docs.text: Harvester_v2 was reached through four design iterations. Each one was built as an anatomy animation to watch a full harvesting cycle before any hardware was made, and each animation exposed a weakness that the next design fixed. The animations below follow that path in order. The full reasoning is in 3. Design Development.

docs.title: Design 1: Fork-Lift Harvester
docs.text:
The conveyor brings a row of lettuce to a fork on a lift unit. The tines slide under the heads, a fixed waterjet cuts the stems, and the fork lifts and turns the row so a comb strips the heads down a chute into a collection bin.

Download the video. Design 1 anatomy animation: conveyor, fork on the lift, chute and collection bin.

The second animation shows the fork turning through 135° to tip the heads onto the comb and chute. A 135° turn sweeps less space than a full rotation, but the motor has to stop and reverse every cycle. Watching it also showed the main problems with Design 1: nothing holds the heads while the fork moves, and they land in a heap in the bin.

Download the video. Design 1 anatomy animation with the 135° flip: heads tipped off the fork, down the chute and into the bin.

docs.title: Design 2: Two-Axis Gantry
docs.text:
Design 2 removes the flip and the comb. A gantry over the end of the conveyor moves the fork on two axes: it slides under the front row, the jet cuts the stems, the vertical axis lifts the row level, and the horizontal axis carries it over the chute to release the heads. The heads stay level, but they still ride loose on the tines and still drop into the bin, and the machine now needs two coordinated motors and a bigger frame.

Download the video. Design 2 anatomy animation: the fork lifts the row level and carries it over the chute.

docs.title: Design 3: Single Cup Holder
docs.text:
Design 3 changes the question from "how do we lift the row?" to "what should hold each head while it is cut?". A split, funnel-shaped cup waits beneath the head, with an S-curved rail on each side. As the plant moves forward, the rails guide the outer leaves up and inward so the head enters the cup without being squeezed. A rack and pinion closes the two cup halves around the stem, and the jet cuts just below, leaving the roots behind while the head stays upright.

Download the video. Single cup holder anatomy animation: S-curved rails, funnel cup and rack-and-pinion closing.

docs.title: Design 4: Multiple Cup Holders
docs.text:
A single cup harvests only one head per cycle. The multi-cup version puts four cups on one shared rack, each with its own pair of S-curved rails. One pinion closes all the cups together and one waterjet line cuts under every stem, so a whole row is harvested per cycle while each head is still held on its own.

Download the video. Multiple cup holders anatomy animation: four cups closed by one pinion, with one jet line under the row.

docs.title: Final Design: Harvester_v2
docs.text: The multi-cup holder was then built into a station over the conveyor, with three cups per row at 300 mm pitch. After the cut the cups open and each head tips forward onto the tray, so nothing drops into a chute. See the System Overview for the final design animation.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text:
Harvester_v2 is a harvesting station that sits over ArianeTech's existing tray conveyor. It holds each lettuce head by the base of its stem in a split cup, cuts the stem with a waterjet, and sets the head back down on the tray, so the leaves are never gripped and nothing drops into a chute.

Download the video. Harvester_v2 final design animation: trays of lettuce move along the conveyor under the harvesting station.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The conveyor indexes the next row of lettuce in, 300 mm at a time.
  2. S-curved rails lift the outer leaves, and the stems slide into the open cups.
  3. One gearmotor drives two opposed racks, closing all three cups together around the stems.
  4. A single waterjet sweeps under the cups and cuts the stems.
  5. The cups open and each head tips forward onto the tray, leaving the root stub behind.

docs.title: Key figures
docs.text:
Heads per row 3, at 300 mm pitch Simulated cycle About 8 s per row Simulated rate About 1,350 heads per hour, 13–18 times the manual rate Cut One waterjet below the cups; no blades touch the crop

For the full design development, see 3. Design Development.

docs.title: Design 1 in motion
docs.text:
Harvester_v2 grew out of Design 1, the fork-lift harvester. In Design 1 the conveyor carries the lettuce to a fork on a lift unit inside the blue frame, a fixed waterjet cuts the stems, and the heads are stripped down a chute into a collection bin. Its problems with loose heads and the drop into the bin led to the later designs (Section 3.3).

Your browser cannot play this video. Download the motion study video. SolidWorks motion study of Design 1: conveyor, lift unit in the blue frame, discharge chute and collection bin.
